en: First of all, the yogi should go for refuge to the Three Jewels. Therein [follows] the confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, dedication, the offering of one's own person, the generation of the mind of compassion, taking recourse in the path, and the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
*Oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness).
*Oṃ sumbha nisumbha hūṃ phaṭ*. *Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ phaṭ*. *Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ phaṭ*. *Oṃ ānaya hoḥ bhagavan vidyārāja hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

From the radiation [of light] arises the vajra-fence, the vajra-canopy, and the vajra-jewel; the earth, black and having the luster of a bow; the wind-maṇḍala, red and triangular; the fire-maṇḍala, red and triangular; the green, square earth-maṇḍala; Mount Sumeru with eight facets; and upon the universal-petal lotus, the mass of the vowels and consonants, transformed from the two rows of vowels, which has come into being.

The lunar and solar mandalas are transformed into the syllable *hūṃ*, upon which stands the Lord Śrī Heruka, with his two feet placed upon Bhairava and Kālarātri. He embraces Vajravārāhī, who is red in color, naked, with disheveled hair, slightly terrifying with her fangs, and who has stepped upon his right thigh. She is adorned with a great passion-red necklace, earrings, a neck-ornament, a crest-jewel, a sacred thread, and smeared with ashes, and is decorated with the six mudrās. His two arms hold a vajra and a vajra-bell.

[He is] red with the saffron of the *hārā* that has stepped upon his right thigh... [he is] covered with the dust of ashes... In his left hand is a skull-cup filled with blood, and in the right a *vajra*; on both hands are the threatening fingers (*tarjanī*); on his feet are bone anklets; his waist is encircled by a garland of *gharghara* bells; and by the two hands of the Lord [is held] the *gaṇaja*...

He wears a garment of human skin; in his right hands he holds a battle-axe, a trident, a curved knife, and a *ḍamaru* drum; in his left hands he holds a *khaṭvāṅga*, a skull-cup, a noose, and the head of Brahmā. He has four faces with knitted brows and a distorted countenance, his tongue lolling out, and his body is like the darkness of smoke. He wears a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), his head is adorned with a garland of skulls, his waist is encircled by a garland of severed heads, and at the top of his matted hair-crown is a universal vajra (*viśvavajra*). His limbs are adorned with a garland of fifty heads strung together with intestines, and he is decorated with the six mudrās.

On the eastern lotus petal is Ḍākinī; on the north, Lāmā; on the west, Khaṇḍarohā; and on the south, Rūpiṇī. In the remaining four petals situated at the intermediate directions are skull-cups filled with the five nectars. The Yoginīs have in their hands a khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, and a knife; they are red in color, naked, with disheveled hair, adorned with the six mudrās, and their feet are slightly in a dancing posture.

On the eastern spoke of the wheel is Mahāvīryā and Vairocana; on the northern spoke is Cakravartinī and Padmanṛtyeśvara; on the western spoke is Suvīrā and Śrīvajragarbha; on the southern spoke is Cakravartinī and Heruka; on the northeastern spoke is Sauṇḍinī and Ākāśagarbha; on the northwestern spoke is Khaṇḍarohā and Hayagrīva; on the southwestern spoke is Cakravegā and Ratnanetra (Vajra); on the southeastern spoke is Prabhāvatī and Mahābala. This is the Mind Wheel (*cittacakra*).

On the eastern spoke of the wheel is Hayakarṇā and Virūpākṣa; on the northern spoke, Subhadrā and Bhairava; on the western spoke, Śyāmādevī and Vajraprabha; on the southern spoke, Surābhakṣī and Vajrahūṃkāra; on the northeastern spoke, Vāyugovā and Mahāvīra; on the northwestern spoke, Mahābhayā and Vajrajaṭila; on the southwestern spoke, Bhairavā and Aṅkurika; and on the southeastern spoke, Airāvatī and Vajradeha. These belong to the wheel of speech.

On the eastern spoke of the vajra [and on the inner spoke of the wheel] is Drumacchāyā with Vajraprabha; on the northern spoke is Laṅkeśvarī with Amitābha; on the western spoke is Śaṅkarī with Surāvairin; on the southern spoke is Vīramatī with Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin; on the northeastern spoke is Mahānāsā with Kaṅkāla; on the northwestern spoke is Prabhāvatī with Mahākaṅkāla; on the southwestern spoke is Caṇḍākṣī with Ruṭaṅkaṭa; and on the southeastern spoke [and on the inner southeastern spoke] is Pracaṇḍā with Khaṇḍakapāla. These belong to the body wheel (*kāyacakra*).

The Yoginīs have skull-bowls and flaying knives in their hands, are red in color, naked, with disheveled hair, adorned with the six mudrās, and hold vajras and vajra-bells in their hands. All these deities, beginning with Śrī Heruka, are established in union, possess three eyes, and stand in the pratyālīḍha posture.

At the eastern gate is Kākāsyā; at the northern gate, Ulūkāsyā; at the western gate, Śvānāsyā; at the southern gate, Śūkarāsyā; in the northeast, Yamadāḍhī; in the northwest, Yamadūtī; in the southwest, Yamadaṃṣṭrī; and in the southeast, Yamamathanī. These Yoginīs hold skull-bowls and flaying knives in their hands, are red in color, naked, with disheveled hair, and adorned with the six mudrās. (In the mantra for the earthen [image]: *kaṭa* by means of one's own self?)

On the eastern spoke of the *kāyacakra* is Pullīramalaya; on the northern spoke, Jālandhara; on the western spoke, Godāvarī; on the southern spoke, Rāmeśvara; on the northeastern spoke, Devīkoṭa; on the northwestern spoke, Mālava; on the southeastern spoke, Oḍiyāna.

On the eastern spoke of the *cittacakra* is Triśakuni; on the northern spoke, Kośala; on the western spoke, Kaliṅga; on the southern spoke, Lampāka; on the northeastern spoke, Kāñcī; on the northwestern spoke, Pretādhivāsinī; on the southwestern spoke, Himālaya; and on the southeastern spoke, Gṛhadevatā.

On the eastern spoke of the wheel of speech is Saurāṣṭra; on the northern spoke, Sindhu; on the western spoke, Maru; on the southern spoke, Kulatā; on the northeastern spoke, Nagara; on the northwestern spoke, Āraṇya; on the southwestern spoke, Suvarṇadvīpa; and on the southeastern spoke, Oḍraviṣaya.
These ten—the Pīṭha, Upapīṭha, Kṣetra, Upakṣetra, Chandoha, Upachandoha, Melāpaka, Upamelāpaka, Śmaśāna, and Upaśmaśāna—are purified.

Oṃ haḥ, *namaḥ* to the heart; hi, *svāhā* to the head; oṃ hu, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock; oṃ he, *hūṃ hūṃ* to the two shoulders; ho, *vauṣaṭ* to the two eyes; āḥ phaṭ phaṭ haṃ, the armor for all limbs. Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra of the Dharmadhātu.
Thus is the ritual procedure for the sequence of the Yoginī’s movement.
In the year [measured by] the sky, arrows, and tastes (1505), in the month of Caitra, during the dark fortnight,
on the day of the Viśvā lunar mansion (the 13th tithi), under the Śatabhiṣaj-Brahmā yoga, on a Wednesday, during the day.
He has written down the *tantra* of Heruka with the foot of the Jina; it is the remover of all defilements and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This manuscript, titled *Yoginīsaṃcāra*, has been written by me.
By this merit, may all people attain every accomplishment (*sarvasiddhi*). May there be auspiciousness!
